newsitem.title: MOROCCO: FEATURE - Morocco's bourse move reflects aim for change.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Morocco's bourse move reflects aim for change.

text.p: Early hours of the trading day see Moroccan stockbrokers on the Casablanca stock exchange at work in the grey-carpeted hush of electronic trading in their nine-storey building.
The new, blue glass home of the bourse inaugurated last month mirrors an eagerness by the exchange to start an era of more transparent trading.

But at 10.15 a.m. each day, after trading on computers from 8.30 a.m., the stockbrokers from the 13 approved firms hit their final button and head for the old exchange building to return to the outcry system of buying and selling.

The bourse was set up by the French in 1929 and progressed slowly in the traditionally conservative Arab country. But with the start of privatisation in 1993 the volume of shares and bonds traded, and the bourse capitalisation, has soared.
"Our new headquarters and the modern equipment are meant to give greater security to investors and traders," said Abderrazak Laraki, general manager of the Moroccan Bourse.
But to keep disruption to a minimum, change to electronic trading is being done slowly. At the moment the stockbrokers deal in just four companies' shares using the computers.
More are to be introduced over the coming weeks but at present the shares in the remaining 43 listed companies are traded under the outcry system.
"From 8.30 to 10.15 brokers feed their computers with orders, then they leave for the outcry market," Laraki said.
The old exchange, about two km (1.25 miles) away, rings with the stockbrokers' voices from 11 a.m. until 12.30 p.m.
OLD MIXES WITH NEW
The visual image of the new exchange, drawn above the entrance, of an olive tree half natural and half stylised, is to represent the mixture of tradition and modernity.
It is a mix that has followed the changeover, and which means more than just a shift to another building and computers for the stockbrokers and exchange staff of 55.
The rules too are being changed, said Laraki.

"With the new electronic system, all traders will introduce their orders at once and then the main computer core will calculate a balance price, satisfying the greatest number of demands and offers," Laraki said.
Shares in Banque Morocaine du Commerce Exterieur -- one of the exchange's most liquid stocks -- are traded continuously with new orders changing the share price.
"There is a first price with first orders. Then with new orders there are new prices, so there can be seven or eight prices during the preopening (8.30-10.15) session," Laraki said.

Shares in the other three firms on computer -- fertilizer firm Fertima, steel mill Sonasid and Samir oil refiney -- are traded on a price fixed for the session at the start of trading after brokers have fed in orders.
"All orders are introduced and there is only one price during the whole session," Laraki said.
Later, as other firms' shares are introduced, medium-liquid stocks will be subject to multi-fixing through the session.

Trading under the outcry system has no fixing, with offer and demand affecting prices during the session. But there is a limit on fluctuations allowed on the official market -- a three percent cap up or down in any one session.

"On the official market there is a three percent floor and ceiling caps authorised. If it goes beyond, it remains reserved (not traded) until a balance is reached during the next two or three sessions," Laraki said.
This rule does not apply to the over-the-counter market where the volume of transactions usually far exceeds trade on the official market.
"The actual over-the-counter market destined for bloc trade has no ceiling or floor caps and no minimum volume of shares giving access to it," said Hicham Saadani, a broker at ABN-AMRO Finance.
But the bourse is looking to change this.
Rules now under debate state an increase or fall must not go beyond five percent of prices on the official market and a minimum number of shares will be needed to trade on it, he added.
GROWTH ON THE BOURSE
Growth on the bourse can be seen from its capitalisation.

In March 1997 it stood at 110.7 billion dirhams ($11.7 billion) from 54.24 billion dirhams in March last year. Only four years ago, in March 1993, capitalisation was 18.57 billion dirhams, according to stock exchange figures.
Turnover this March was four billion dirhams, from 3.7 billion in March 1996 and 98.75 million dirhams in March 1993.
Who invests?
"Morocco's bourse relies for at least 80 percent on local investors," Laraki said. "Foreigners are easily disheartened, any small thing can make them withdraw their funds and leave.
"Of course foreign funds are necessary to a country's development, but it's not like an infrastructure project where people have to stay until it is finished. They can leave any time."
